opening.text: Imagine a man who wants to learn from a wise teacher. The teacher pours him a cup of tea. The man holds out his cup, and the teacher keeps pouring. The tea spills over the rim and runs across the table. The man jumps back. "Stop! The cup is full!"
The teacher smiles. "Yes. And so are you. How can I teach you anything, if you are already full?"
That old story says something true about humility. A full cup cannot be filled. A person who thinks they already know everything has no room to learn.

mainMessage.text: Humility is not thinking badly of yourself. It is not weakness, and it is not shyness. Humility is being teachable. It is knowing that God is greater than we are, and that we need Him every day.
The gospel teaches that humility opens the door to everything good. It invites the Spirit. It brings us closer to others. It lets the Savior's grace work in us.

We will look at six parts today. What humility is. What pride does. How humility helps us in weakness. How it keeps us teachable. How it shapes the way we treat others. And how it leads us to the Savior.

blocks.text: Let us begin with the Savior's own words. His disciples had been arguing about who was the greatest. Jesus called a little child to stand in the middle of them.

And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.

Become as little children. Not childish, but childlike. A little child trusts. A little child asks questions. A little child does not pretend to know what he does not. And the greatest in the kingdom, Jesus says, is the one who humbles himself like that.
King Benjamin taught the same thing. He said we must put off our natural selfish ways.

For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.

Here is a list. Submissive. Meek. Humble. Patient. Full of love. Willing to submit. These are the marks of a person who has yielded to the Holy Spirit. Notice that it says becometh. It is a process. We do not wake up humble. We grow into it through the Atonement of Christ.

President Ezra Taft Benson, who served as President of the Church, gave one of the clearest definitions of humility. He did it by naming its opposite. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:
The antidote for pride is humility—meekness, submissiveness (see Alma 7:23). It is the broken heart and contrite spirit (see 3 Nephi 9:20; 12:19; D&C 20:37; 59:8; Psalm 34:18; Isaiah 57:15; 66:2).

The antidote for pride. That is a good picture. Pride is a kind of poison, and humility is the cure. And the cure is the broken heart and contrite spirit. It means we come to God with an empty cup, ready to receive what He gives.
What happens when the cup is full of ourselves? The scriptures speak plainly about pride.
Solomon wrote a short warning that has been quoted for three thousand years.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Before a fall. Pride does not just feel bad. It sets us up to be hurt. When we think we are above correction, above counsel, above needing anyone, we stop watching where we step.
James explained what is at stake.
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.

God resisteth the proud. That is a hard sentence. But look at the other half. He giveth grace unto the humble. Grace is the help and strength that come from God. The humble receive it. The proud turn it away.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency described how pride shows up in real life. In his talk "Pride and the Priesthood," from the October 2010 general conference, he said:

At its core, pride is a sin of comparison, for though it usually begins with 'Look how wonderful I am and what great things I have done,' it always seems to end with 'Therefore, I am better than you.' . . . This is the sin of 'Thank God I am more special than you.' At its core is the desire to be admired or envied. It is the sin of self-glorification.

A sin of comparison. Most of us do not think of ourselves as proud. But many of us compare. We measure our house, our children, our calling, our talents against someone else's. And when we come out ahead, we feel good. When we come out behind, we feel bitter. Both are pride. Both fill the cup with ourselves.
Here is the good news. Humility does not leave us weak. It makes room for the strength of God.
The Lord taught Moroni this truth in a time when Moroni felt his own weakness.

And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.

I give unto men weakness that they may be humble. That is a surprising idea. Our weaknesses are not accidents. They are invitations. When we see how much we need Him, we turn to Him. And then He makes weak things become strong.
The Lord gave another promise in the early days of the Church.
Be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers.

Lead thee by the hand. Think of a child crossing a busy street. The parent takes the child's hand. The child does not need to know the way. The child only needs to hold on. That is what humility looks like.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke about humility in hard times. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The Lord will give relief with divine power when you seek deliverance in humility and faith in Jesus Christ. Don't say, 'No one understands me; I can't sort it out, or get the help I need.' Those comments are self-defeating. No one can help you without faith and effort on your part. Your personal growth requires that.

Humility and faith. Those two go together. Humility says, I cannot do this alone. Faith says, but He can. And Elder Scott warns against the opposite voice, the one that says no one understands me. That voice keeps the cup closed. The humble person lets help come in.
Now think about the empty cup again. To stay teachable, we have to keep pouring out what we think we already know. How do we do that?
Alma taught the poor among the Zoramites something about choosing humility. They had been humbled by their circumstances. He wanted them to see there was a better way.

And now, as I said unto you, that because ye were compelled to be humble ye were blessed, do ye not suppose that they are more blessed who truly humble themselves because of the word?
Yea, he that truly humbleth himself, and repenteth of his sins, and endureth to the end, the same shall be blessed—yea, much more blessed than they who are compelled to be humble because of their exceeding poverty.
Therefore, blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble; or rather, in other words, blessed is he that believeth in the word of God, and is baptized without stubbornness of heart, yea, without being brought to know the word, or even compelled to know, before they will believe.
There are two ways to become humble. We can be compelled by hard times, or we can choose it. Alma says the second way is more blessed. Humble yourself without waiting to be forced.
President Benson picked up this very point. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:

God will have a humble people. Either we can choose to be humble or we can be compelled to be humble. Alma said, 'Blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble' (Alma 32:16). Let us choose to be humble.
Let us choose. It is a decision. No one can make us humble in the way that matters, though life may try. The humbling that blesses us is the one we choose.
Pride has a sound, and President Henry B. Eyring of the First Presidency described it. In his talk "Prayer," from the October 2001 general conference, he said:
Pride creates a noise within us which makes the quiet voice of the Spirit hard to hear. And soon, in our vanity, we no longer even listen for it. We can come quickly to think we don't need it.

A noise within us. A full cup makes a noise when it sloshes. We stop hearing the quiet voice. And soon we do not even listen. The humble person is quiet inside. That quiet lets the Spirit speak. If you want to hear the Spirit more clearly, one place to start is to lower the noise of your own pride.
Humility changes how we treat other people. It is hard to look down on someone when we are kneeling beside them.
Paul wrote to the saints at Philippi about this.

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:

In lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. That does not mean pretending others are better in every way. It means we stop competing. We look at the other person and see someone worth honoring. And we look not only at our own things, but at the things of others.
President Uchtdorf explained why pride damages our relationships. In the same talk, "Pride and the Priesthood," he said:

When our hearts are filled with pride, we commit a grave sin, for we violate the two great commandments \[see Matthew 22:36–40\]. Instead of worshipping God and loving our neighbor, we reveal the real object of our worship and love—the image we see in the mirror.

The image we see in the mirror. That is a sharp line. When pride rules, we have made ourselves the center. We stop loving God and stop loving our neighbor. Humility turns us around. It points us outward.
President Benson gave practical ways to choose humility. In "Beware of Pride," he said:
We can choose to humble ourselves by forgiving those who have offended us (see 3 Nephi 13:11, 14; D&C 64:10). We can choose to humble ourselves by rendering selfless service (see Mosiah 2:16–17).
Forgiving. Serving. Two things that make pride uncomfortable. When we forgive, we give up our right to be right. When we serve, we put someone else first. Both empty the cup.
Where does humility lead? To the Savior, who is our perfect example.
He spoke these words to anyone weighed down by life.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart. The Son of God describes Himself that way. The most powerful being in the universe chose to be meek. And He invites us to learn from Him. A person who is humble enough to learn will find rest.
Peter, who knew what it was to be humbled, gave a promise.
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:
He may exalt you in due time. The Lord lifts those who bow. Not on our schedule, and not for our pride. But in due time. It is a promise that the humble are never forgotten.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when humility made a difference in their life. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Naaman and the River Jordan

blocks.text: Naaman was a great captain in the army of Syria. He was also a leper. A servant girl told him of a prophet in Israel who could heal him. Naaman traveled to Elisha. But Elisha did not come out. He sent a messenger who said, go wash in the Jordan seven times. Naaman was furious. He expected something grand. He turned to leave. Then his servants spoke up.

And his servants came near, and spake unto him, and said, My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean? Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.

Naaman's cup was full of his own ideas. He wanted a different cure. But when he humbled himself and did the simple thing, he was healed. And look at the result. His flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child. Humility made him like a child again, and made him clean. Sometimes what the Lord asks of us is simple. The hard part is the pride that says it is too simple.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, empty the cup. Pick one area where you think you already know the answer. A parenting habit, a work method, a view about someone. Ask the Lord what you might be missing.
Second, choose humility. Do one thing that Benson listed. Forgive someone, or give selfless service. Do it before anyone makes you.
Third, quiet the noise. Spend ten minutes in silence before the Lord. Do not ask for anything. Just listen. Let the noise of pride settle, and see what the Spirit says.

closingVerse.text: And behold, I tell you these things that ye may learn wisdom; that ye may learn that when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.

opening.text: In Bethlehem, there is an old church built over the place where Jesus is believed to have been born. To go inside, you have to pass through a door. The door is very small. It is so low that every visitor, even a tall one, has to bow to get through.

The door was made that way on purpose. Long ago, it was made smaller so that people would not ride in on horses. Today it works as a teacher. No one walks into that place standing tall. Everyone bows.
That is a good picture of humility. We cannot go through the door to the Savior with our heads held high.

mainMessage.text: When we hear the word humble, we sometimes think of someone small, quiet, or timid. But humility is not about being small. It is about being honest. It is seeing ourselves as we are, and seeing God as He is. We are His children, and we need Him. He is our Father, and He is able to help.
Humility is the low door into every blessing the Lord has for us. It opens the way to His Spirit, His grace, and His guidance.

We will walk through six parts. What humility is. What pride does. How humility turns weakness into strength. How it keeps us listening. How it shapes our love for others. And how it brings us to Christ.

blocks.text: Let us start with what the Savior taught. His disciples came to Him and asked who was the greatest. He answered with a child.

And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.

Except ye become as little children. A child fits through low doors easily. A child does not mind asking for help. A child is not worried about looking foolish. That is the spirit Jesus is asking for. And the one who humbles himself like that is the greatest.
King Benjamin described what that child-like spirit looks like.

For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.

Submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love. That is how the saint looks. And it is a becoming. The verse says that it happens through the Atonement of Christ. We do not make ourselves humble by trying hard. We yield to the Spirit, and He changes us.
President Ezra Taft Benson, who was then the President of the Church, defined humility by naming what it cures. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:
The antidote for pride is humility—meekness, submissiveness (see Alma 7:23). It is the broken heart and contrite spirit (see 3 Nephi 9:20; 12:19; D&C 20:37; 59:8; Psalm 34:18; Isaiah 57:15; 66:2).

A broken heart and a contrite spirit. This is the sacrifice the Lord asks for. Not a loud one. Not a showy one. A softened heart. And that, President Benson says, is the cure for pride. It is a low door that anyone can walk through.
Why does the gospel make such a point of this? Because pride closes the door.
Solomon gave us a sentence that has lasted for centuries.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Before a fall. A person with a haughty spirit is not looking down at where they step. They are looking at themselves. And that is when we trip.
James gave the same message from a different angle.
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.

God resisteth the proud. He does not pour His grace into a full cup. But He gives it freely to the humble. That means every person has the same access to grace. The only difference is whether we bow to receive it.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency described a form of pride that many of us miss. In his talk "Pride and the Priesthood," from the October 2010 general conference, he said:

At its core, pride is a sin of comparison, for though it usually begins with 'Look how wonderful I am and what great things I have done,' it always seems to end with 'Therefore, I am better than you.' . . . This is the sin of 'Thank God I am more special than you.' At its core is the desire to be admired or envied. It is the sin of self-glorification.

The desire to be admired or envied. That is something many of us feel. Social media, work, even church can make us want to be seen as better. But look at where it ends. Therefore, I am better than you. And that thought builds a wall between people. It makes the door high and wide for us, and narrow for everyone else.
So what do we do about our weakness? Pretend it is not there? The Lord has a better plan.
He told Moroni something about weakness that has encouraged many people since.

And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.

I will show unto them their weakness. This is the Lord's kindness. He does not shame us. He shows us where we need Him. And then He promises grace that is sufficient. If we humble ourselves and have faith, weak things become strong.
The Lord made a further promise to a servant in the early Church.
Be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers.
Lead thee by the hand. That is how a loving parent walks a small child through a low door and across a dark room. We do not have to see the whole path. We only have to hold the hand.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke on how humility helps in hard times. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The Lord will give relief with divine power when you seek deliverance in humility and faith in Jesus Christ. Don't say, 'No one understands me; I can't sort it out, or get the help I need.' Those comments are self-defeating. No one can help you without faith and effort on your part. Your personal growth requires that.

Seek deliverance in humility and faith. Not in anger. Not in pride. When we are in pain, there is a temptation to say no one understands. Elder Scott says that those words close the door. Humility opens it. It says, Lord, I need help, and I will do my part.
The low door also teaches us to stay listening. A humble person keeps learning. How do we keep that spirit?
Alma spoke to a group of poor people who had been humbled by hardship. He wanted them to see that there was more than one way to be humble.

And now, as I said unto you, that because ye were compelled to be humble ye were blessed, do ye not suppose that they are more blessed who truly humble themselves because of the word?
Yea, he that truly humbleth himself, and repenteth of his sins, and endureth to the end, the same shall be blessed—yea, much more blessed than they who are compelled to be humble because of their exceeding poverty.
Therefore, blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble; or rather, in other words, blessed is he that believeth in the word of God, and is baptized without stubbornness of heart, yea, without being brought to know the word, or even compelled to know, before they will believe.

Without stubbornness of heart. That phrase is worth holding on to. A humble person is not stubborn. When the word of God comes, they believe it, even before they have seen the proof. They bow before they are made to.
President Benson made this a call to every one of us. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:

God will have a humble people. Either we can choose to be humble or we can be compelled to be humble. Alma said, 'Blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble' (Alma 32:16). Let us choose to be humble.
Either we choose it, or we are compelled. Most of us have felt both. Hard times can humble us. But the better way is to bow on our own, before the door gets any lower.
President Henry B. Eyring of the First Presidency spoke of what pride does to our hearing. In his talk "Prayer," from the October 2001 general conference, he said:
Pride creates a noise within us which makes the quiet voice of the Spirit hard to hear. And soon, in our vanity, we no longer even listen for it. We can come quickly to think we don't need it.

We can come quickly to think we don't need it. That is how fast it happens. One day we feel strong, and the next we stop listening for the Spirit. The humble person keeps listening, because they know they need help every day.
What does humility do for our love of others? It lets us see them clearly.
Paul wrote to the saints at Philippi and gave them a way of looking at each other.

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory. That would clear up a lot of meetings, a lot of families, and a lot of workplaces. And in lowliness of mind, esteem others better. Look on the things of others. Humility turns our eyes outward.
President Uchtdorf said that pride does the opposite. In his talk "Pride and the Priesthood," he said:

When our hearts are filled with pride, we commit a grave sin, for we violate the two great commandments \[see Matthew 22:36–40\]. Instead of worshipping God and loving our neighbor, we reveal the real object of our worship and love—the image we see in the mirror.

The real object of our worship. That is strong language, and it is meant to wake us. Pride quietly makes us the god of our own small world. Humility restores the right order. God first, then our neighbor.
President Benson gave us ways to practice this. In "Beware of Pride," he said:
We can choose to humble ourselves by forgiving those who have offended us (see 3 Nephi 13:11, 14; D&C 64:10). We can choose to humble ourselves by rendering selfless service (see Mosiah 2:16–17).
Two concrete steps. Forgive. Serve. Notice that both involve another person. We cannot learn humility only in private. We learn it by bending toward others.
And where does the low door lead? To Jesus Christ.
He described Himself in a way that surprises many people.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
Meek and lowly in heart. He is the King of kings, and He calls Himself lowly. And He says, learn of me. If we want to be humble, we have the best teacher. And the reward is rest for our souls.
Peter, who had once denied the Lord and been forgiven, wrote a promise to the saints.
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:
Under the mighty hand of God. That is a safe place to bow. The hand that holds us is mighty and kind. And in due time, it lifts us up. We do not bow to be crushed. We bow to be lifted.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they chose to bow instead of resist. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Mary says yes

blocks.text: Mary was a young woman in Nazareth. An angel came to her with news that was beyond anything she had imagined. She would bear the Son of God. She did not have a plan for how this would happen. She had many questions, and the angel answered some. And then she gave her answer.
And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her.

Behold the handmaid of the Lord. She called herself a servant. She did not say, why me, or let me think about it. She said, be it unto me according to thy word. That is humility. It is not weakness. It took great strength to say yes to something so large. It was the humility of someone who trusts God more than her own plan.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, bow at the door. Start each morning with a short kneeling prayer. Tell the Lord you need Him today. It takes one minute, and it changes the way the day starts.
Second, esteem another. Pick one person you tend to compare yourself with. This week, find one thing about them you can honestly admire, and tell them.
Third, say yes to the Lord. Is there something He has asked of you that you have been putting off? Say what Mary said. Be it unto me according to thy word. Then take the first step.

opening.text: Drive past a wheat field in late summer and look closely. Some stalks stand straight and tall. They look proud. But walk up and lift one. It is empty. The heads that are full of grain hang low. They bend over because they are heavy with what they carry.
Farmers have known this for ages. The full head bows. The empty one stands up straight.

I think that is a good picture of humility. A humble person is not someone with nothing to offer. It is someone full enough to bow. They carry real gifts, real work, real faith. And they bow anyway, because they know where it all came from.
Today I want us to look at what makes a heart bend like that, and why the Lord loves it so much.

mainMessage.text: Humility is not thinking less of yourself. It is knowing who God is and who you are in front of Him. It means you accept that every good thing you have is a gift, and that you still need Him every day.
The world often tells us to stand tall and stand alone. The gospel teaches a different strength. It is the strength of the ripe head of wheat. It bows, and it feeds many.

In this talk we will look at six things. First, why Jesus used a child to teach us. Second, why pride costs us so much. Third, how weakness can become strength. Fourth, how we keep our hearts soft. Fifth, how humility changes the way we treat others. And sixth, where it all leads us, to the Savior.

blocks.text: The disciples once asked Jesus who was greatest in the kingdom of heaven. It was a natural question for ambitious men. His answer must have surprised them. He called a little child to stand in front of them.

And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
Think about a small child. A child does not pretend to know everything. A child asks for help without shame. A child trusts the people who love them. That is the pattern the Lord wants us to follow.
King Benjamin taught the same thing, and he added what is at stake.

For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.

See the words he uses. Submissive. Meek. Humble. Patient. Full of love. That is a list of qualities most of us would like to have. And notice that we do not get them by trying harder on our own. We get them when we yield to the Holy Spirit and rely on the Atonement of Christ.
President Ezra Taft Benson, President of the Church, gave a clear warning and a clear answer. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:
The antidote for pride is humility—meekness, submissiveness (see Alma 7:23). It is the broken heart and contrite spirit (see 3 Nephi 9:20; 12:19; D&C 20:37; 59:8; Psalm 34:18; Isaiah 57:15; 66:2).

An antidote is what you take when something is poisoning you. Pride is a poison. Humility is the cure. And the cure is a broken heart and a contrite spirit. That means a heart that is open to God, not closed and defended.
Like the wheat, the child does not bow because it is small. The child bows because it knows it is not the source of its own life.
Now let us talk about the stalk that stands straight because it is empty. That is what pride looks like.
Solomon wrote it plainly.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Pride does not announce itself. It often feels like confidence or self-respect. But it has a hidden cost. It always sets us up to fall, because it takes our eyes off God and puts them on ourselves.
James said it even more directly.
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.

God resisteth the proud. That is a sobering thought. But look at the other half. He giveth grace unto the humble. The same God who stands against pride runs to help the person who bows. Every one of us wants that grace. And here is how to receive it.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf explained what pride really is. In his talk "Pride and the Priesthood," from the October 2010 general conference, he said:

At its core, pride is a sin of comparison, for though it usually begins with 'Look how wonderful I am and what great things I have done,' it always seems to end with 'Therefore, I am better than you.' . . . This is the sin of 'Thank God I am more special than you.' At its core is the desire to be admired or envied. It is the sin of self-glorification.

A sin of comparison. That is a helpful way to see it. Pride is not only about being proud of what we have. It is about measuring ourselves against others. We can be proud of being better. We can also be proud in a quiet way about being worse, as if our troubles make us special.
In a field, no stalk of wheat is better than another because it stands higher. What matters is what it carries. When we stop comparing, we are free to simply grow and give.
Here is something that may surprise you. The Lord does not ask us to pretend we are strong. He asks us to be honest about our weakness. That is where His power starts.
Moroni was worried about his weakness in writing. The Lord answered him with a promise.

And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.

I give unto men weakness that they may be humble. Our weaknesses are not a mistake. They are a door. When we see them honestly and bring them to Him, He makes weak things strong. Not by removing every weakness at once, but by giving us His grace.
To the early Church leaders, the Lord gave a short instruction that has helped many people since.
Be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers.
Be humble. Then He leads by the hand. He answers prayers. That is a simple deal, and a good one. The hand that leads is kind and steady.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke to those who are struggling. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The Lord will give relief with divine power when you seek deliverance in humility and faith in Jesus Christ. Don't say, 'No one understands me; I can't sort it out, or get the help I need.' Those comments are self-defeating. No one can help you without faith and effort on your part. Your personal growth requires that.
Humility and faith, together. Humility says, I need help. Faith says, He can give it. And the effort is ours. The wheat does not grow without sun, but it must also send roots down. Both parts matter.
A ripe head of wheat stays soft only while it keeps its place in the field. So how do we keep our hearts soft?
Alma told a crowd that humility can come two ways. One is forced. The other is chosen.

And now, as I said unto you, that because ye were compelled to be humble ye were blessed, do ye not suppose that they are more blessed who truly humble themselves because of the word?
Yea, he that truly humbleth himself, and repenteth of his sins, and endureth to the end, the same shall be blessed—yea, much more blessed than they who are compelled to be humble because of their exceeding poverty.
Therefore, blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble; or rather, in other words, blessed is he that believeth in the word of God, and is baptized without stubbornness of heart, yea, without being brought to know the word, or even compelled to know, before they will believe.
The forced kind is a blessing too. But the chosen kind is greater. It is the wheat that bends in the breeze, not the wheat flattened by a storm.
President Benson put it in a way we can all remember. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:

God will have a humble people. Either we can choose to be humble or we can be compelled to be humble. Alma said, 'Blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble' (Alma 32:16). Let us choose to be humble.
Let us choose. The choice is ours today. We do not have to wait for a crisis.
President Henry B. Eyring of the First Presidency told us what happens when we do not choose it. In his talk "Prayer," from the October 2001 general conference, he said:
Pride creates a noise within us which makes the quiet voice of the Spirit hard to hear. And soon, in our vanity, we no longer even listen for it. We can come quickly to think we don't need it.

A noise within us. Many of us know that noise. It is the voice that says, I can handle this. I already know. Humility turns that noise down, and then we can hear the quiet voice again. That is why humble people tend to be well guided. They are listening.
Humility is never only about us. It shows up in how we treat the people near us. Paul gave the Philippians a very practical teaching.

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:

Esteem other better than themselves. That does not mean we pretend we have no talent. It means we stop treating every conversation as a contest. We look for what others do well. We take interest in what matters to them.
President Uchtdorf showed what is at stake. In his talk "Pride and the Priesthood," he said:

When our hearts are filled with pride, we commit a grave sin, for we violate the two great commandments \[see Matthew 22:36–40\]. Instead of worshipping God and loving our neighbor, we reveal the real object of our worship and love—the image we see in the mirror.
He is saying that pride and love cannot live in the same heart. A full head of wheat leans toward the ground. A proud heart leans toward itself. When we turn the lean outward, we begin to love.
President Benson then gave us two ways to start. In "Beware of Pride," he said:
We can choose to humble ourselves by forgiving those who have offended us (see 3 Nephi 13:11, 14; D&C 64:10). We can choose to humble ourselves by rendering selfless service (see Mosiah 2:16–17).
Forgiving is hard because pride says, they owe me. Serving is hard because pride says, my time is too valuable. Both are cured by the same thing. A humble heart.
Is there someone you need to forgive this week? Is there someone you could quietly help? Those are the places where humility becomes real.
All of this leads us to the Savior. He is the one who bent lowest, and He is the one who lifts us.
He invites us to come close and learn from Him.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

A yoke is what ties two animals together to pull a load. When He says, take my yoke upon you, He is saying, come pull beside me. He is meek and lowly. He walks at our pace and carries the heavy end. That is what humility looks like in the Savior.
And Peter gives the promise that follows.
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:

In due time. We do not need to push ourselves up. The harvest comes in its season. The head that bows is gathered in. The empty stalk is left standing in the field. When we bow, God does the lifting, and He does it better than we could.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they stepped back so someone else could shine. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: John the Baptist steps aside

blocks.text: John the Baptist had a large following. People came from all over to hear him and be baptized. Then Jesus began to teach, and people began to leave John and go to Him. Some of John's own disciples were upset by this. John was not. He told them why.
He must increase, but I must decrease.

John knew his work. He was the one who prepared the way. When the One he had been preparing for arrived, he was glad to move aside. He did not feel smaller. He felt complete. This is a true picture of humility. It does not need the spotlight, because it knows who the light is.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, name the gift. Write down three good things you are able to do. Then, next to each, write who helped you get there. This helps your heart bend the way ripe wheat does.
Second, turn down the noise. When you notice yourself saying, I already know this, stop for a moment. Ask, what could I learn here? Then listen.
Third, step aside for someone. This week, let another person take the credit, the first turn, or the last word. Do it quietly. Notice how it feels.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that God gives grace to the humble. I know that our weakness is not our end. When we bring it to Him, He makes it strength. I have felt the peace that comes when I stop trying to carry everything alone and let the Savior carry it with me. I know that He lives and that He loves each of us. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to write down three things you do well and who helped you get there.
I invite you to pause when you catch yourself thinking, "I already know this," and ask what you could learn.
I invite you to let someone else take the credit or the first turn.
blessings: You will find joy in lifting others.

closingVerse.text: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;

opening.text: A potter sits at the wheel with a lump of wet clay. He presses his thumbs into the center and the clay begins to rise. It can become a bowl, a jug, or a lamp. It all depends on one thing. Is the clay soft?

If the clay is dry and hard, nothing can be done. It cracks when the potter presses. It will not take a shape. But soft clay can become something useful and beautiful, because it lets the potter's hands do their work.
You and I are that clay. The Lord is the potter. And the question He asks every day is the same. Are you soft?
That is what humility means. It is a heart soft enough to be shaped.

mainMessage.text: Pride makes a heart hard. It says, I have already become who I want to be. Humility makes a heart soft. It says, Lord, make me into what you want.
None of us is finished. The Lord knows that, and He is patient. But He can only shape what will yield to Him. The more we yield, the more we become.

Today we will look at six parts of this. First, what the Lord asks of a soft heart. Second, what happens when a heart hardens. Third, why weakness is not the problem. Fourth, how to stay soft. Fifth, how a soft heart treats others. And sixth, the Potter Himself.

blocks.text: When the disciples asked who was greatest, Jesus did not give a rank. He gave a picture of a child.

And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
A child is clay in the best sense. Easy to teach. Quick to ask. Quick to forgive. Not worried about looking foolish. The Lord says we must become like that if we want to enter His kingdom.
King Benjamin explained how this change happens.

For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.
The key word is yields. The natural man in us does not yield. The saint does. And a saint is not made by our own strength. It happens through the Atonement of Christ.
President Ezra Taft Benson, President of the Church, taught what to reach for. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:
The antidote for pride is humility—meekness, submissiveness (see Alma 7:23). It is the broken heart and contrite spirit (see 3 Nephi 9:20; 12:19; D&C 20:37; 59:8; Psalm 34:18; Isaiah 57:15; 66:2).

A broken heart sounds painful. But think of the potter again. Before the clay can be shaped, it has to be worked and softened. A broken heart is one that has been softened enough to be formed. It is not a ruined heart. It is a ready one.
What happens when a heart will not soften? The Bible has a clear answer.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.

Hard clay cracks. That is what a fall looks like. It does not usually come all at once. It starts as a small refusal to be taught, then a refusal to listen, then a refusal to repent. And then, one day, something breaks that did not need to break.
James adds the heavenly view.
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
God resisteth the proud. Not because He is unkind. It is because pride shuts the door that grace walks through. A closed hand cannot receive a gift.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf helped us see how pride works. In his talk "Pride and the Priesthood," from the October 2010 general conference, he said:

At its core, pride is a sin of comparison, for though it usually begins with 'Look how wonderful I am and what great things I have done,' it always seems to end with 'Therefore, I am better than you.' . . . This is the sin of 'Thank God I am more special than you.' At its core is the desire to be admired or envied. It is the sin of self-glorification.

A sin of comparison. Imagine two bowls on a shelf, each one saying, I am the better bowl. The potter made them both. He does not rank them the way they rank each other. He just wants them to hold water.
If you notice yourself comparing, that is a sign the clay is starting to dry. It is a good time to go back to the Potter.
Many people think the problem is that they are not strong enough. The Lord sees it differently. He has a promise for the person who admits their weakness.

And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.

Look at what He does. He shows us our weakness. That is not to shame us. It is to help us see where His hands can work. Then He gives grace, and weak things become strong. Clay that is humble before the potter can hold water. Clay that thinks it needs no potter ends up in pieces.
To Joseph Smith and the early Saints, the Lord gave a short, steady promise.
Be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers.
Lead thee by the hand. Hands are the potter's tool. They are gentle, and they know the shape the clay is meant to take. If we stay humble, we are in those hands.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave us a way to receive help. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The Lord will give relief with divine power when you seek deliverance in humility and faith in Jesus Christ. Don't say, 'No one understands me; I can't sort it out, or get the help I need.' Those comments are self-defeating. No one can help you without faith and effort on your part. Your personal growth requires that.

Notice the last two sentences. No one can help without faith and effort on your part. Even soft clay has to stay on the wheel. We do our part, which is to stay, to ask, and to try. The Lord does His part, which is the shaping.
A pot that has been shaped still needs care. If it sits in the sun too long, it hardens again. So how do we keep a heart soft?
Alma taught that we can choose to bend, or we can wait until we are forced.

And now, as I said unto you, that because ye were compelled to be humble ye were blessed, do ye not suppose that they are more blessed who truly humble themselves because of the word?
Yea, he that truly humbleth himself, and repenteth of his sins, and endureth to the end, the same shall be blessed—yea, much more blessed than they who are compelled to be humble because of their exceeding poverty.
Therefore, blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble; or rather, in other words, blessed is he that believeth in the word of God, and is baptized without stubbornness of heart, yea, without being brought to know the word, or even compelled to know, before they will believe.
Without stubbornness of heart. That is the soft clay. It does not wait for the fire to be told. It believes the word and acts on it.
President Benson put the choice before us. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:

God will have a humble people. Either we can choose to be humble or we can be compelled to be humble. Alma said, 'Blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble' (Alma 32:16). Let us choose to be humble.
Some of us have been compelled. We know what it feels like. But there is a gentler road, and it is open today.
President Henry B. Eyring of the First Presidency warned about what dries our hearts out. In his talk "Prayer," from the October 2001 general conference, he said:
Pride creates a noise within us which makes the quiet voice of the Spirit hard to hear. And soon, in our vanity, we no longer even listen for it. We can come quickly to think we don't need it.

We can come quickly to think we don't need it. A hardening heart rarely feels hard. It feels capable. It feels fine. That is why daily prayer matters. When we kneel, we put ourselves back on the wheel.
Soft clay does something else. It fits with other pieces. A proud heart is hard and has sharp edges. A soft heart makes room.
Paul wrote to the Philippians about this.

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:

Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus. We are not asked to invent humility. We are asked to copy His. Notice how He treated people. He listened. He noticed the one who was overlooked. He served at the last supper with a towel and a basin.
President Uchtdorf named the cost of pride in our love. In his talk "Pride and the Priesthood," he said:

When our hearts are filled with pride, we commit a grave sin, for we violate the two great commandments \[see Matthew 22:36–40\]. Instead of worshipping God and loving our neighbor, we reveal the real object of our worship and love—the image we see in the mirror.
That is a hard line to read. It does not sound gentle. But it is meant as a warning from a friend. If the mirror is where we look most, we are missing God and everyone else.
President Benson gave two practical habits. In "Beware of Pride," he said:
We can choose to humble ourselves by forgiving those who have offended us (see 3 Nephi 13:11, 14; D&C 64:10). We can choose to humble ourselves by rendering selfless service (see Mosiah 2:16–17).
Forgive. Serve. These are the potter's two favorite tools. Forgiveness softens the old hard places. Service shapes us into something useful.
Think of a small thing you can do for someone today. Do it without telling anyone. That alone will teach you more than a lesson can.
And who is the Potter? He is the Savior, and He describes Himself in a way that gives us courage.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

Meek and lowly in heart. If we were going to put our lives in someone's hands, we would want those hands to be gentle. His are. He is not harsh. He does not shame the clay for being clay. He invites us to come and rest.
Peter gave a promise to anyone who comes.
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:

The mighty hand of God. A potter's hand is strong, but the strength is used to form, not to crush. He may exalt you in due time. A finished vessel is lifted from the wheel and put in a place of honor. That is the end of the story He has in mind for us.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they realized they had been hard and chose to soften. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The Pharisee and the publican

blocks.text: Jesus told a story to people who trusted in themselves and looked down on others. Two men went to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee. He stood and listed all his good works and thanked God that he was not like other men. The other was a publican, a tax collector, whom most people disliked. He stood far away. He would not even lift his eyes.

And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.

The Pharisee had a lot to say, and he was already full of himself. The publican had one short prayer, and it was true. He left with something the Pharisee did not get. Soft clay can be shaped. Hard clay goes home just as it came.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, get back on the wheel. Pray each morning and each night. In each prayer, ask one question: Lord, what do you want me to learn or change?
Second, find the hard place. Think of one person you have not forgiven, or one habit you have not wanted to give up. Name it to the Lord. Ask Him to soften it.
Third, do one quiet service. Choose something you can do for someone this week without being thanked. Let it be between you and the Lord.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that the Lord is patient with us. I know that He shapes our lives with great care, and that He can make something good out of weak things. I have felt Him soften my heart when I was ready to listen. I know that Jesus Christ is meek and lowly, and that His hands are safe to rest in. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to pray each morning and night and ask, "Lord, what do You want me to learn or change?"
I invite you to name one grudge or habit to the Lord and ask Him to soften it.
I invite you to do one quiet act of service without being thanked.
blessings: You will be shaped by the Lord.

closingVerse.text: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.

opening.text: Go out on a clear night, far from the city lights. Look up. You will see thousands of stars. Most of them you cannot see in town. They were there all along. The city lights simply drowned them out.
Something like that happens in our hearts. The Lord is always speaking. His light is always there. But when our own lights are too bright, with our plans, our pride, and our noise, we cannot see Him.
Humility is like switching off the lights. Nothing new appears. What was always there becomes clear.
Today we will talk about how to turn our own lights down, so we can see what God has been showing us.

mainMessage.text: We are small. That is not an insult. It is simply true, and it is a relief. We are not the center, and we do not have to hold up the sky. God does that. Our part is to look up, trust, and follow.

Humility is seeing ourselves and God as we truly are. He is great and loving. We are His children, small and dearly loved. When we see this, the fear and the comparing fade, and peace grows in their place.

We will look at six things. First, the child the Savior pointed to. Second, the glare of pride. Third, how weakness lets in light. Fourth, how to stay in the dark enough to see. Fifth, how humility makes us kind. And sixth, the Savior, who is the light we are looking for.

blocks.text: Jesus once answered a question about greatness by placing a child in the middle of the room.

And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
Children look up all the time. They have to. Everything they need is above their heads. They ask, they trust, and they wonder. The Lord asks us to keep that posture, even as adults.
King Benjamin taught what this kind of life looks like.

For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.

He says the natural man is an enemy to God until he yields. That is a strong statement. But the way out is gentle. We yield to the enticings of the Holy Spirit. We do not fight our way into sainthood. We let ourselves be drawn.
President Ezra Taft Benson, President of the Church, gave the cure. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:
The antidote for pride is humility—meekness, submissiveness (see Alma 7:23). It is the broken heart and contrite spirit (see 3 Nephi 9:20; 12:19; D&C 20:37; 59:8; Psalm 34:18; Isaiah 57:15; 66:2).
A broken heart and a contrite spirit. These are not signs of defeat. They are the dark sky that lets the stars show. When we are not full of ourselves, we have room to see Him.
Pride is the glare. It outshines everything else, and it keeps us from seeing what matters.
Solomon warned us about where the glare leads.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
When we are dazzled by our own light, we stumble. We do not see the step. A fall comes, and we are surprised, because we thought we could see.
James tells us what God does about it.
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.

God resisteth the proud. Think of it as a gentle push back. He will not let our small light take the place of His great one. But to the humble He gives more grace. When we step into the dark, He fills it.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf described the glare well. In his talk "Pride and the Priesthood," from the October 2010 general conference, he said:

At its core, pride is a sin of comparison, for though it usually begins with 'Look how wonderful I am and what great things I have done,' it always seems to end with 'Therefore, I am better than you.' . . . This is the sin of 'Thank God I am more special than you.' At its core is the desire to be admired or envied. It is the sin of self-glorification.

Here is something to think about. Stars do not compare themselves with each other. Each one simply shines where it is. When we stop measuring ourselves against others, we can shine too, without needing to outshine anyone.
You might think that our weaknesses are the part of us that block the light. The Lord teaches the opposite. They are where the light comes in.

And if men come unto me I will show unto them their weakness. I give unto men weakness that they may be humble; and my grace is sufficient for all men that humble themselves before me; for if they humble themselves before me, and have faith in me, then will I make weak things become strong unto them.

I give unto men weakness that they may be humble. It is a kind gift. Our weakness reminds us to look up. If we were strong in everything, we would never feel the need. But because we are not, we turn to Him, and His grace is enough.
The Lord has also given a direct word to those who want guidance.
Be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers.

Travelers once crossed deserts and seas by the stars. They did not make the stars. They only looked up and followed. In the same way, the Lord leads the humble by the hand, and answers prayers. We do not need to be brilliant. We need to be willing.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said something to those who feel stuck. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The Lord will give relief with divine power when you seek deliverance in humility and faith in Jesus Christ. Don't say, 'No one understands me; I can't sort it out, or get the help I need.' Those comments are self-defeating. No one can help you without faith and effort on your part. Your personal growth requires that.
The night sky is always there, but you have to go outside to see it. That is the effort. Humility and faith bring us outside, and then divine power does the rest.
How do we stay in the dark enough to see the stars? We choose to step away from our own glare, on purpose and often.
Alma taught that this can be a choice or something that happens to us.

And now, as I said unto you, that because ye were compelled to be humble ye were blessed, do ye not suppose that they are more blessed who truly humble themselves because of the word?
Yea, he that truly humbleth himself, and repenteth of his sins, and endureth to the end, the same shall be blessed—yea, much more blessed than they who are compelled to be humble because of their exceeding poverty.
Therefore, blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble; or rather, in other words, blessed is he that believeth in the word of God, and is baptized without stubbornness of heart, yea, without being brought to know the word, or even compelled to know, before they will believe.

Sometimes a power outage is what makes people look up at the stars. They notice what they had been missing. Hard times can do that for us. But Alma says there is a greater blessing for those who turn the lights down themselves.
President Benson called us to make the choice. In his talk "Beware of Pride," from the April 1989 general conference, he said:

God will have a humble people. Either we can choose to be humble or we can be compelled to be humble. Alma said, 'Blessed are they who humble themselves without being compelled to be humble' (Alma 32:16). Let us choose to be humble.
What would choosing look like for you this week? It may be as simple as putting your phone down and sitting in quiet for ten minutes. It may be asking someone for advice and truly listening.
President Henry B. Eyring of the First Presidency explained what blocks the Spirit. In his talk "Prayer," from the October 2001 general conference, he said:
Pride creates a noise within us which makes the quiet voice of the Spirit hard to hear. And soon, in our vanity, we no longer even listen for it. We can come quickly to think we don't need it.
Noise and glare are two sides of the same thing. Both hide what is quiet and steady. When we choose quiet, we hear the Spirit. And when we hear Him, we find He had been speaking all along.
When we see ourselves rightly, we see others rightly too. Every person is a child of God, as small and loved as we are.
Paul taught the Philippians how to treat each other.

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:

Look not every man on his own things. If we are always watching our own small light, we miss the others. Humility lets us look around. We see that the person next to us has a story, a struggle, and a gift.
President Uchtdorf showed what pride does to love. In his talk "Pride and the Priesthood," he said:

When our hearts are filled with pride, we commit a grave sin, for we violate the two great commandments \[see Matthew 22:36–40\]. Instead of worshipping God and loving our neighbor, we reveal the real object of our worship and love—the image we see in the mirror.
When the glare is on, the only thing we can see is the mirror. But when the lights go down, we see God above us and our neighbor beside us. That is the right order, and it is where love lives.
President Benson then gave two ways to put this into practice. In "Beware of Pride," he said:
We can choose to humble ourselves by forgiving those who have offended us (see 3 Nephi 13:11, 14; D&C 64:10). We can choose to humble ourselves by rendering selfless service (see Mosiah 2:16–17).
Forgive someone. Serve someone. Neither has to be big. A kind message, a ride, a meal, a quiet apology. These small acts are how humble people live.
And the light we are looking for is the Savior. The stars point to Him.
He said something about Himself that we should hold close.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
The greatest light in the universe says He is meek and lowly. He does not blind us. He draws us in gently. And He offers rest, which is something most of us need.
Peter gave a promise to anyone who answers that invitation.
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:
Under the mighty hand of God. That hand holds the stars in place. It can hold us too. And He will lift us in due time. We do not need to climb. We only need to look up and trust.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they trusted the Lord's power more than their own. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The centurion

blocks.text: A Roman centurion came to Jesus in Capernaum. He was a commander of soldiers, used to giving orders. But his servant was very sick, and there was nothing he could do. So he came to Jesus. Jesus offered to come to his house. The centurion said no.

The centurion answered and said, Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: but speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed.
For I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me: and I say to this man, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth it.
When Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.

Here was a powerful man who knew the difference between his authority and the Savior's. He said, I am not worthy. And he said, speak the word only. The Lord marvelled at his faith. Humility and faith went together. He looked up and trusted, and he saw what he needed.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, find your quiet. Choose a time each day to sit without a screen for ten minutes. Use it to pray and listen.
Second, look at someone else. Pick one person and ask them a real question about their life. Then listen to the whole answer without waiting to speak.
Third, speak the centurion's words. When you face something you cannot fix, say, Lord, I am not worthy, but speak the word only. Then take the next step you know to take.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that God is great and that He knows each of us. I know that when we are humble, we can see His hand in our lives. I have found that the stars were always there. I only had to look up. I know that Jesus Christ is the light of the world, and that He invites us to come to Him and rest. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
